WHAT CHANGED
- Ask the six questions and summarize the answers in Alex’s own words.
- Choose three titles believed to be available on Netflix US.
- Let Alex decide how to balance the preferences; there is no shared step-by-step choosing method.
- Allow a brief reaction before each next question in the one-at-a-time format.

BEFORE
This was the starting version, before the numbered changes.

WHY WE TRIED IT
Establish how often the two formats naturally agreed before trying to make their choices more consistent.

EXAMPLE (ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT A RECORDED REPLY)
Two people giving the same answers could receive two different sets of three recommendations because Alex was free to decide how to balance their preferences.

WHAT CHANGED
- Use the recently enjoyed title as the strongest clue to taste, including its genre, style, country, or language.
- Respect the requested movie/show format, available time, and things the person wants to avoid.
- Exclude titles the person has already seen and prefer widely known choices.
- Mention all six answers in the same question order in the summary.
- In the one-at-a-time format, ask only the next question. Remove reactions and thanks between answers.

BEFORE
The starting version described the task but left Alex considerable freedom over how to choose the three titles.

WHY WE TRIED IT
Reduce differences caused by either version inventing its own choosing method or adding extra conversational comments.

EXAMPLE (ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT A RECORDED REPLY)
If the person enjoyed a Korean drama, both versions should consider similar Korean dramas. After a genre answer, the one-at-a-time version should ask the mood question directly, without an extra reaction.

WHAT CHANGED
- Accept “idk,” “anything,” “whatever,” and “no” as answers. Continue instead of asking the question again.
- Among suitable titles, prefer the three most famous or most widely watched.
- Change the usual temperature setting from 0.2 to 0 to try to reduce variation.
- A separate website setting could still replace that value. The actual live value was not checked.

BEFORE
Vague answers could still lead to inconsistent handling, and the popularity instruction only said to prefer popular titles.

WHY WE TRIED IT
Keep both conversations moving through the same questions and give Alex a clearer way to choose between similar options.

EXAMPLE (ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT A RECORDED REPLY)
“Anything” counts as an answer. If several titles fit equally well, Alex should favor the ones it believes more people have watched, rather than choosing freely.

WHAT CHANGED
- Pick 1: choose the closest match to the recently enjoyed title.
- Pick 2: choose a popular title that matches the preferred genre and current mood.
- Pick 3: choose a different title that fits the requested movie/show format and available time.
- When two choices seem equally good, prefer the more widely watched one.

BEFORE
Alex was choosing three generally suitable titles without a separate purpose for each position.

WHY WE TRIED IT
Try to make the choice more repeatable by telling Alex exactly what each of the three positions should accomplish.

EXAMPLE (ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT A RECORDED REPLY)
The first pick is the closest to the favorite; the second is there because it matches genre and mood; the third is there because it fits the format and time. These are three different reasons for inclusion.

WHAT CHANGED
- Propose a prewritten, ranked menu of titles grouped by genre.
- Use the Korean-drama list for a Korean favorite; otherwise start with the first genre named.
- Skip titles that conflict with the requested format, things to avoid, or titles already seen. Take the first three remaining entries.
- Do not use mood or time to choose from the menu. Tell the one-at-a-time version to read all six answers together when choosing.
- Reject and remove this fixed-menu proposal before testing it; restore the earlier choosing rules.
- The restored instructions include a reminder to consider the six answers together. No evaluation ran for the fixed menu.

BEFORE
Alex could choose from titles it knew, using the selection rules from Eval #3.

WHY WE TRIED IT
A fixed menu could make matching easier, but it would also restrict what Alex was allowed to recommend. That approach was not accepted.

EXAMPLE (ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT A RECORDED REPLY)
Instead of thinking of three suitable comedies, Alex would work down a prewritten comedy list and take the first three allowed entries. This approach was never measured.

WHAT CHANGED
- Remove the separate job assigned to each recommendation.
- Copy all six answers, in order, into a “Got it” line. Use that written summary when choosing.
- Choose three well-known titles that fans of the recently enjoyed title might watch next.
- Keep the movie/show and avoidance checks. Do not recommend the enjoyed title itself.
- Explicitly stop using mood and available time to choose titles.
- If no favorite is named, use the first genre; if no genre is named either, use general Netflix US popularity.
- Remove the extra instruction to read the answers together; the copied summary now serves that purpose.

BEFORE
The three picks had different jobs, including matching mood and available time.

WHY WE TRIED IT
Reduce the number of competing preferences Alex had to balance and give both formats the same written summary before choosing.

EXAMPLE (ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT A RECORDED REPLY)
Alex could repeat “I want something light” and “I have one hour” in the summary, while still choosing mostly from fans’ next-watch options for the favorite. Repeating an answer did not mean it was used to choose the titles.

WHAT CHANGED
- Replace “what fans watch next” with titles similar in genre, kind of story, and country or language.
- Write the guide sentence before the picks: “Since you liked [title], here are 3 picks most like it:”.
- Copy the exact wording and capitalization of every answer in the “Got it” line.
- Keep movie/show and avoidance checks. A match to mood, time, or a separately named genre alone is not enough; the favorite remains the main choosing guide.
- If no favorite is given, use popular choices in the first genre, or overall popularity if no genre is given.

BEFORE
Alex was choosing what fans of the favorite might watch next, which could include titles that were not very similar.

WHY WE TRIED IT
Make the reason for choosing the recommendations more specific and have Alex state that reason before producing the list.

EXAMPLE (ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT A RECORDED REPLY)
“Other titles fans watch” becomes “other titles with a similar story and feel.” For a Korean drama, the instruction now explicitly points toward a similar kind of Korean story.

WHAT CHANGED
- Look first for titles from the same series, fictional world, or creators as the favorite.
- Then consider popular titles with a similar genre and story. If equally close, favor the more widely watched one.
- If the person says “either” or gives no clear format, make every pick the same format as the favorite.
- Keep the copied-answer line and the guide sentence before the picks.

BEFORE
Alex looked for similarity to the favorite, but several kinds of similarity could compete. A person saying “either” could receive a mixture of movies and shows.

WHY WE TRIED IT
Give Alex a clearer order for searching for choices and remove movie-versus-show uncertainty when the answer is “either.”

EXAMPLE (ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT A RECORDED REPLY)
If the favorite is a TV show and the person says “either,” all three picks should be TV shows. A related series or a show by the same creators gets considered before a less directly related title.

WHAT CHANGED
- Keep the Eval #7 prompt instructions unchanged.
- Always send temperature 0, even if a different temperature is set elsewhere.
- Add a fixed seed of 368: a repeatability setting intended to make choices steadier.
- These are software settings, not new questions or choosing rules. They do not guarantee identical replies.

BEFORE
The temperature setting could be replaced by a website setting, and no repeatability seed was being sent.

WHY WE TRIED IT
Check whether changing the model-request settings, rather than adding more instructions, would make the two formats agree more often.

EXAMPLE (ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT A RECORDED REPLY)
The person answers exactly the same questions and Alex reads exactly the same instructions as in Eval #7. Only the settings accompanying the request change. This is a settings round, not a new question or choosing rule.

WHAT CHANGED
- Give early priority only to sequels, prequels, and spin-offs from the same series or fictional world.
- Remove “same creators” from that first-priority group. After related stories, use popular titles with a similar genre and story.
- Add a final check that none of the recommendations repeats the enjoyed title.
- If no favorite is named, use popular Netflix original TV series in the first genre, or overall if no genre is given.
- The Netflix-original restriction applies only to the no-favorite case in this round, not to all recommendations.

BEFORE
Being made by the same creators was enough to give a title early priority, even if it was a different kind of story. The no-favorite choices were broader.

WHY WE TRIED IT
Make the first choices more directly related to the favorite and reduce the number of possible choices when the person gives little information.

EXAMPLE (ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT A RECORDED REPLY)
A spin-off of the favorite gets early priority. A completely different show by the same creator no longer gets that priority simply because of who made it.

WHAT CHANGED
- Keep similarity and related-story rules for picks 1 and 2.
- For pick 3, choose another well-known title by the creator or director of pick 1.
- If that creator has no other suitable title in the required format, use the creator or director of pick 2 instead.
- Also exclude specials, documentaries, and behind-the-scenes programs about the favorite. Keep the final check against repeating the favorite.

BEFORE
All three recommendations were chosen mainly for resemblance to the person’s favorite.

WHY WE TRIED IT
Try a specific rule for the third pick, which otherwise had several plausible alternatives.

EXAMPLE (ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT A RECORDED REPLY)
After choosing recommendation A, Alex should look at who made A and choose another title by that person for pick 3. This refers to the maker of the first recommendation, not automatically the maker of the participant’s favorite.

WHAT CHANGED
- Remove the special creator/director rule for pick 3. Return all three picks to similarity and related-story rules.
- Write the three numbered title lines together, with no explanation between them.
- Put the explanations after the full list. Begin each explanation with its title name and do not number it.

BEFORE
Each title was followed immediately by its explanation, and the third pick followed Eval #10’s creator/director rule.

WHY WE TRIED IT
Try choosing the entire three-title list before writing explanations that might influence later choices. Since the third-pick rule was also removed, the round does not isolate the effect of reply order alone.

EXAMPLE (ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT A RECORDED REPLY)
Before: title A, explanation A, title B, explanation B, title C. After: title A, title B, title C, followed by all three explanations.

WHAT CHANGED
- Allow only titles described as Netflix originals for all three picks.
- Choose well-known originals similar to the favorite. Prefer the more popular title when two are equally close.
- Remove the special priority for sequels and related fictional worlds.
- Put each explanation directly under its title again.
- Keep the format and avoidance checks, plus exclusions for the favorite and programs about it.
- Remove the separate final-check sentence, while keeping the rule against recommending the favorite.
- If no favorite is given, continue using popular Netflix original series.

BEFORE
Recommendations could include titles Netflix streamed without making or releasing them as originals. Related stories received special priority, and explanations appeared after the full title list.

WHY WE TRIED IT
Give Alex fewer possible titles and a shorter set of choosing rules to follow. This also changes the range of recommendations the person can receive.

EXAMPLE (ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT A RECORDED REPLY)
A suitable title would now be excluded if it did not count as a Netflix original under the prompt’s rule. Matching could improve simply because Alex has a smaller pool of titles to choose from.

WHAT CHANGED
- Write either “3 Netflix original movies” or “3 Netflix original TV shows” in the sentence before the picks.
- Choose one format. If the person says “either,” use the favorite’s format.
- Exclude shows that first aired on a TV network, even if Netflix streams them.
- If there is no favorite, use the first three shows on Netflix’s official all-time “Most Popular English TV” list.
- The app does not look up that list. Alex is instructed to rely on its own knowledge of it.

BEFORE
The Netflix-original and movie/show restrictions were in the instructions, but Alex’s introductory sentence only promised three similar picks.

WHY WE TRIED IT
Have Alex write the key restrictions immediately before naming titles and give the no-favorite case a more specific starting point.

EXAMPLE (ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT A RECORDED REPLY)
The lead-in changes from “here are 3 picks most like it” to “here are 3 Netflix original TV shows most like it.” This makes both the allowed source and the format explicit before the titles appear.

WHAT CHANGED
- When two titles are equally similar to the favorite, choose the earlier release.
- This replaces the previous instruction to choose the more widely watched title in that situation.
- Keep all other Eval #13 instructions and request settings. Release dates still come from Alex’s knowledge, not a lookup.

BEFORE
For two similarly suitable Netflix originals, Alex was told to prefer the one it believed more people had watched.

WHY WE TRIED IT
Try a more specific way to choose between two similar options instead of asking Alex to estimate which is more popular.

EXAMPLE (ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT A RECORDED REPLY)
If one equally suitable title was released in 2018 and another in 2020, the instruction says to choose the 2018 title.

WHAT CHANGED
- Exclude a show that first aired on a TV network in any country, even if Netflix later streams it or calls it an original.
- Use Breaking Bad and Money Heist as examples of titles excluded under this experiment’s rule.
- Keep the earlier-release rule, answer copying, favorite-based similarity, temperature 0, and seed 368.

BEFORE
The prompt excluded shows that first aired on a TV network, but the rule could still be interpreted differently for shows from other countries or later branded by Netflix.

WHY WE TRIED IT
Reduce disagreement about which titles are allowed, rather than changing what kind of story the person wants. This is the definition written into the prompt, not a fresh check of Netflix’s catalog.

EXAMPLE (ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT A RECORDED REPLY)
If a show began on a network outside the US and Netflix later acquired it, Alex should still leave it out under this version of the instructions.

WHAT CHANGED
- Keep both Eval #15 prompts exactly the same.
- Stop sending the seed. Use the website’s temperature setting if present, otherwise 0.2.
- The actual website override was not checked, so the live temperature is not confirmed to have been 0.2.
- After testing, restore temperature 0 and seed 368 in commit 04ac259.

BEFORE
Alex used the Eval #15 prompts while requests always included temperature 0 and seed 368.

WHY WE TRIED IT
Compare the request settings while holding the instructions constant, so this round focuses on settings rather than another wording change.

EXAMPLE (ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT A RECORDED REPLY)
The person sees the same questions and Alex reads the same choosing rules as in Eval #15. Only the settings intended to influence variation are changed; afterwards, the earlier settings are put back.

NOT YET EVALUATED

WHAT CHANGED
- Use all six answers when choosing: requested format and things to avoid first, then similarity to the favorite, then genres and mood, then available time.
- If no favorite is given, choose using genres and mood.
- Remove the Netflix-original-only restriction. Keep the requirement to recommend real, released titles believed available on Netflix US.
- Introduce the picks as “Based on your answers,” rather than “Since you liked [title].”.
- Keep the same six questions. What changes is how their answers guide the picks.
- NEW EVALUATION STILL NEEDED: this latest combination of instructions has not had its own evaluation. Earlier scores do not apply to it.
